Rendered the page to an image (saved as in the same folder) and read it: the English prose of the quote is there verbatim: 'There is a marked disinclination to accent the ultima.. All that can be stated with unqualified certainty is that where q is variable, in those forms in which it is retained, the accent precedes.' The only differences are in the Chinook forms: the report's tgaqa'mstk is printed as tga^a'mstk (superscript glottal-stop sign, not q), and the accent/diacritic renderings are scanned approximations. new_statements.rule_in_words: No source gives a positional rule for Lower Chinook word accent. Accent is a single culminative word accent (Dyk & Hymes 1956: 238 'one phoneme of stress.. apparently in all other Chinookan dialects') whose position is set morphologically: certain suffixes pull it (future -a and distributive -ma toward the end, plural -uks to the penult, -iamt to itself), some nouns keep the stem accent fixed, and vowels (E, a) are inserted purely to carry it. The one general tendency stated (Swanton 1900: 207) is a marked avoidance of final-syllable accent. Boas's phonetics section describes only the effects of accent on vowels and consonants.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Boas 1911 mentions 'secondary accent' once in a morphological gloss (p. 587: 'E with secondary accent becomes a- before n'); no description of secondary-stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Boas 1911: 607 'In a number of words the accent does not shift' under the plural suffix, 'particularly frequent in terms which occur always with possessive pronouns, such as terms designating parts of the body and relationships'; Swanton 1900: 207 gives exceptions to the velar-loss/accent rule ('This rule by no means covers all cases'). Dyk & Hymes 1956: 240 note the future-tense backward accent shift is more regular in Shoalwater Chinook than in Wishram.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms and text forms from one Shoalwater speaker, Charles Cultee; Boas 1911: 564 'practically all our information on the Lower Chinook has been derived from one single individual'). Swanton's analysis is of Boas's published Chinook Texts, not independent fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: All primary data are the Shoalwater (Chinook proper) dialect of Lower Chinook from Charles Cultee (Boas 1911: 563 'The last-named dialect [Chinook proper of the north bank and Shoalwater bay] is discussed here'); Glottolog dialect shoa1234 'Shoalwater' under chin1286. Clatsop (klat1237) is not separately described. Dyk & Hymes 1956 is about Wishram (wasc1239) and is used here only for its explicit comparative remarks on Shoalwater Chinook.

sources.note: Phonetic preliminaries pp. 200-207 (analysis of Boas's Chinook Texts). p. 207: 'There is a marked disinclination to accent the ultima', with the note that velar q is dropped when the accent moves to follow it, that e/i/E are strengthened to a under the accent, and that a or E is 'inserted to carry the accent' when the accent is thrown forward. No positive fixed-position rule.
